title: Walking into an Open-Source Project — urlcat
summary: Most people dream of contributing to open source, then freeze when a project is right in front of them. Today I lucked into a library that felt approachable.
markdown:
Most people dream of contributing to open source, then freeze when a project is right in front of them. Today I lucked into a library that felt approachable — urlcat.

![image]()
Untitled.png

urlcat is only 267 lines of code, yet it has 1.4k stars and over 10k weekly downloads. It is the smallest open-source project I have met so far. Below is a walk through what each file does in the project.

![image]()
Untitled 1.png

## .github

![image]()
image.png

From the names, these are issue and PR templates. The three templates cut communication cost between maintainers and users and speed up problem-solving:

**bug_report.md** asks for:

1. What is wrong
1. How to reproduce
1. Expected behavior
1. Screenshots
1. Desktop environment: OS, browser, version
1. Mobile environment: device, OS, browser, version
1. Context: whether this relates to other issues

**feature_request.md** asks for:

1. Whether the feature ties to a problem
1. The solution you want
1. Alternatives you considered
1. Related feature issues

**pull_request_template.md** asks for:

1. A short summary of the PR
1. A detailed description

## docs

![image]()
image.png

What / Why / How nail the project's reason to exist.

- **What:** what is it?
- **Why:** why build it?
- **How:** how do you use it?

Beyond that, there is detailed API documentation and guidance on how to contribute code.

## src

Where the source lives. I will write a separate post on the source later.

## test

Everyone says unit tests matter; most people also say they take too much time. Even for a few hundred lines, the author still wrote thorough tests. That is an attitude.

## .all-contributorsrc

A project stays alive only when many people keep it moving.

## .editorconfig

Helps keep coding style consistent across editors and IDEs.

```plain text
# Whether this is the top-level config; when true, stop searching parent .editorconfig files
root = true

[*]
# Line ending type
end_of_line = lf
# Whether the file should end with a newline
insert_final_newline = true
# Indent style
indent_style = space
# Indent size
indent_size = 2
# Encoding
charset = utf-8
```

## .eslintignore

Tells ESLint which files and directories to skip.

```plain text
node_modules
dist
coverage
```

## .eslintrc.js

ESLint config:

```javascript
module.exports = {
  env: {
    node: true,
  },
  root: true,
  parser: '@typescript-eslint/parser',
  plugins: ['@typescript-eslint'],
  extends: ['eslint:recommended', 'plugin:@typescript-eslint/recommended'],
  rules: {
    'object-curly-spacing': ['error', 'always'],
    'array-bracket-spacing': ['error', 'never'],
    quotes: ['error', 'single'],
    'no-console': ['error'],
  },
};
```

There are plenty of good ESLint config write-ups; this article is a solid start if you care.

Related:

- ESLint config file `.eslintrc` parameter notes

## .gitignore

Useful when some files should never be committed.

```plain text
/node_modules
/dist
/dist-test
/.nyc_output
/coverage
.vscode
```

## .npmignore

When publishing an npm package, skip files that should not ship to npm.

```plain text
/node_modules
/dist-test
/src
/docs
/test
/.travis.yml
/tsconfig.json
/tsconfig-test.json
/.nyc_output
/coverage
```

## .travis.yml

Config for a continuous integration service:

```yaml
language: node_js
node_js:
  - lts/*
  - 14
  - 13
  - 12
  - 11
  - 10
script:
  - npm run lint
  - npm test
  - npm run coverage
```

For continuous integration, Ruan Yifeng's tutorial is enough.

Related:

- Travis CI continuous integration tutorial

## jest.config.js

Unit test config — another gap of mine; I will study this more later.

```javascript
module.exports = {
  preset: 'ts-jest',
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage',
  collectCoverage: true,
  testMatch: ['**/test/**/*.ts'],
  verbose: true,
  collectCoverageFrom: ['**/src/**/*.ts'],
  testPathIgnorePatterns: ['dist.*\\.ts$'],
};
```

## package-lock.json

In short: lock third-party package versions. Projects depend on many packages that depend on more packages; when an upstream ships a breaking API, a plain `npm install` can surprise you at runtime.

Related:

- npm semantic versioning
- Differences between package-lock.json and yarn.lock dependencies

## package.json

Every frontend person knows this file. A few less-common but important fields:

Pin Node version:

```json
{
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=8 <14"
  }
}
```

Pin npm version:

```json
{
  "engines": {
    "npm": "~1.0.20"
  }
}
```

If you publish an npm package, `files` can help — it lists what goes into the published package.

Hooks: npm scripts support `pre` and `post` hooks that auto-run around special commands, for example:

- Delete `dist` before `build`
- Run tests and build before `publish`

```json
"scripts": {
    "clean": "shx rm -rf dist",
    "prebuild": "npm run clean",
    "build": "tsc -p .",
    "test": "jest",
    "lint": "eslint . --ext .js,.jsx,.ts,.tsx",
    "coverage": "cat ./coverage/lcov.info | coveralls",
    "prepublish": "npm test && npm run build",
    "docs": "docsify serve docs --open"
  },
```

Related:

- package.json in depth
- package.json things you may not know

## renovate.json

A familiar feeling — it's that tool.

![image]()
Untitled 6.png

![image]()
Untitled 7.png

Renovate is an open-source tool that automates:

- Detecting dependencies in a repo (open source and private)
- Checking for updates
- Opening commits and merge/pull requests to bump them
- …and more

Used when the project is written in TypeScript.

## Summary

Aside from the source and unit tests, this post covers what the other files are for. Open source is hard. When we use a library casually, its authors have already put in a lot. A group of people from around the world finishing one thing together — beyond skill, what you see most is attitude.
